claim: CSF is constantly produced by the choroid plexus.
source: CSF is constantly produced by the choroid plexus (Damkier et al., 2013), circulates through the subarachnoid space and into the brain via a periarterial route (Iliff et al., 2012), and then exits the brain via several routes (Weed, 1923; McComb, 1983; Zakharov et al., 2004; Pollay, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Damkier et al., 2013, which provides external evidence for CSF production by the choroid plexus.

claim: CSF circulates through the subarachnoid space and into the brain via a periarterial route.
source: CSF is constantly produced by the choroid plexus (Damkier et al., 2013), circulates through the subarachnoid space and into the brain via a periarterial route (Iliff et al., 2012), and then exits the brain via several routes (Weed, 1923; McComb, 1983; Zakharov et al., 2004; Pollay, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Iliff et al., 2012, which provides external evidence for the periarterial route of CSF circulation.

claim: CSF exits the brain via several routes.
source: CSF is constantly produced by the choroid plexus (Damkier et al., 2013), circulates through the subarachnoid space and into the brain via a periarterial route (Iliff et al., 2012), and then exits the brain via several routes (Weed, 1923; McComb, 1983; Zakharov et al., 2004; Pollay, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Weed, 1923; McComb, 1983; Zakharov et al., 2004; Pollay, 2010) that provide external evidence for multiple CSF exit routes.

claim: Normal aging is accompanied by decreases in CSF production.
source: Normal aging is accompanied by decreases in CSF production and increases in CSF outflow resistance (May et al., 1990; de Leon et al., 2017; Czosnyka et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to May et al., 1990; de Leon et al., 2017; Czosnyka et al., 2004, which provide external evidence for age-related changes in CSF production.

claim: Normal aging is accompanied by increases in CSF outflow resistance.
source: Normal aging is accompanied by decreases in CSF production and increases in CSF outflow resistance (May et al., 1990; de Leon et al., 2017; Czosnyka et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to May et al., 1990; de Leon et al., 2017; Czosnyka et al., 2004, which provide external evidence for age-related changes in CSF outflow resistance.

claim: CSF turnover is disrupted in Alzheimer's disease.
source: CSF turnover is disrupted in pathological conditions such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) and normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) (Albeck et al., 1998; König et al., 2005; Silverberg et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Albeck et al., 1998; König et al., 2005; Silverberg et al., 2006, which provide external evidence for CSF turnover disruption in AD.

claim: CSF turnover is disrupted in normal pressure hydrocephalus.
source: CSF turnover is disrupted in pathological conditions such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) and normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) (Albeck et al., 1998; König et al., 2005; Silverberg et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Albeck et al., 1998; König et al., 2005; Silverberg et al., 2006, which provide external evidence for CSF turnover disruption in NPH.

claim: The balance between CSF production and outflow plays a key role in setting and maintaining intracranial pressure.
source: The balance between CSF production and outflow plays a key role in setting and maintaining the intracranial pressure (ICP) (Kosteljanetz, 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kosteljanetz, 1987, which provides external evidence for the role of CSF balance in ICP regulation.

claim: CSF production is actively regulated to maintain normal ICP.
source: Because CSF production is actively regulated to maintain normal ICP (Marmarou et al., 1975), damage to the outflow pathways could drive compensatory decreases in CSF production and turnover (Czosnyka et al., 2004) or altered patterns of CSF flow.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Marmarou et al., 1975, which provides external evidence for active regulation of CSF production.

claim: Damage to CSF outflow pathways could drive compensatory decreases in CSF production and turnover.
source: Because CSF production is actively regulated to maintain normal ICP (Marmarou et al., 1975), damage to the outflow pathways could drive compensatory decreases in CSF production and turnover (Czosnyka et al., 2004) or altered patterns of CSF flow.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Czosnyka et al., 2004, which provides external evidence for compensatory mechanisms following outflow pathway damage.

claim: There are lymphatic vessels in the meninges.
source: While there are lymphatic vessels in the meninges (Aspelund et al., 2015; Louveau et al., 2015), there is evidence in both humans and other mammals pointing to drainage of the CSF through the cribriform plate (CP) (Zakharov et al., 2004; de Leon et al., 2017; Walter et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2019; Bradbury et al., 1981; Erlich et al., 1986; Yamada et al., 1991; Cserr and Knopf, 1992a; Weller et al., 1992; Kida et al., 1993; Boulton et al., 1996; Johnston et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aspelund et al., 2015; Louveau et al., 2015, which provide external evidence for meningeal lymphatic vessels.

claim: There is evidence in both humans and other mammals pointing to drainage of CSF through the cribriform plate.
source: While there are lymphatic vessels in the meninges (Aspelund et al., 2015; Louveau et al., 2015), there is evidence in both humans and other mammals pointing to drainage of the CSF through the cribriform plate (CP) (Zakharov et al., 2004; de Leon et al., 2017; Walter et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2019; Bradbury et al., 1981; Erlich et al., 1986; Yamada et al., 1991; Cserr and Knopf, 1992a; Weller et al., 1992; Kida et al., 1993; Boulton et al., 1996; Johnston et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Zakharov et al., 2004; de Leon et al., 2017; Walter et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2019; Bradbury et al., 1981; Erlich et al., 1986; Yamada et al., 1991; Cserr and Knopf, 1992a; Weller et al., 1992; Kida et al., 1993; Boulton et al., 1996; Johnston et al., 2004) that provide external evidence for CSF drainage through the cribriform plate.

claim: The cribriform plate is a fenestrated bony plate of the ethmoid bone that separates the cranial and nasal cavities.
source: The CP is a fenestrated bony plate of the ethmoid bone that separates the cranial and nasal cavities.
evidence: The claim is a direct anatomical description stated in the manuscript, representing established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Once through the cribriform plate, CSF is absorbed by lymphatic vessels in the nasal mucosa and drained into the cervical lymph nodes.
source: Once through the plate, CSF is absorbed by lymphatic vessels in the nasal mucosa and drained into the cervical lymph nodes (Bradbury and Cole, 1980).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bradbury and Cole, 1980, which provides external evidence for CSF absorption and drainage pathways.

claim: ISF and CSF may leave the brain via the extracellular space between olfactory sensory nerve axon bundles.
source: There has been speculation that interstitial fluid (ISF) and CSF leave the brain via the extracellular space between olfactory sensory nerve (OSN) axon bundles (Szentistvanyi et al., 1984), as the intercellular space between axon bundles provide low-resistance directed pathways for fluid flow (Syková and Nicholson, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Szentistvanyi et al., 1984 and Syková and Nicholson, 2008, which provide external evidence for this hypothesis.

claim: The intercellular space between axon bundles provides low-resistance directed pathways for fluid flow.
source: There has been speculation that interstitial fluid (ISF) and CSF leave the brain via the extracellular space between olfactory sensory nerve (OSN) axon bundles (Szentistvanyi et al., 1984), as the intercellular space between axon bundles provide low-resistance directed pathways for fluid flow (Syková and Nicholson, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Syková and Nicholson, 2008, which provides external evidence for the fluid flow properties of intercellular spaces.

claim: Acute blockage of CSF outflow by surgically obstructing the cribriform plate results in an increase in resting ICP.
source: Acute blockage of CSF outflow by surgically obstructing the CP results in an increase in resting ICP (Mollanji et al., 2002) and outflow resistance (Silver et al., 2002), providing evidence for a drainage role of the trans-CP pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mollanji et al., 2002, which provides external evidence for ICP changes following CP obstruction.

claim: Acute blockage of CSF outflow by surgically obstructing the cribriform plate results in increased outflow resistance.
source: Acute blockage of CSF outflow by surgically obstructing the CP results in an increase in resting ICP (Mollanji et al., 2002) and outflow resistance (Silver et al., 2002), providing evidence for a drainage role of the trans-CP pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Silver et al., 2002, which provides external evidence for outflow resistance changes following CP obstruction.

claim: There may be a connection between the patency of the clearance pathway through the cribriform plate and neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Intriguingly, there may be a connection between the patency of the clearance pathway through the CP and neurodegenerative diseases (de Leon et al., 2017; Ethell, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to de Leon et al., 2017; Ethell, 2014, which provide external evidence for a potential connection between CP clearance and neurodegeneration.

claim: OSNs are exposed to environmental toxins such as air pollutants.
source: The neurons whose axons make up the nerve bundles that traverse the CP, OSNs, are exposed to environmental toxins (such as air pollutants [Ajmani et al., 2016]), which epidemiological studies have associated exposure to neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ajmani et al., 2016, which provides external evidence for OSN exposure to air pollutants.

claim: Epidemiological studies have associated exposure to air pollutants with neurodegenerative diseases.
source: The neurons whose axons make up the nerve bundles that traverse the CP, OSNs, are exposed to environmental toxins (such as air pollutants [Ajmani et al., 2016]), which epidemiological studies have associated exposure to neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ajmani et al., 2016, which provides external evidence for epidemiological associations between air pollutants and neurodegeneration.

claim: Anosmia and decreased acuity in the sense of smell reliably precede many neurological disorders.
source: Furthermore, anosmia and decreased acuity in the sense of smell, which will result from OSN damage, reliably precede many neurological disorders (Ajmani et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ajmani et al., 2016, which provides external evidence for anosmia as a precursor to neurological disorders.

claim: Damage to or decreases in the numbers of OSN axons could increase the resistance to CSF outflow.
source: Thus, damage to or decreases in the numbers of the OSN axons could increase the resistance to CSF outflow, triggering a downregulation in CSF production and turnover.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on logical inference from the anatomical role of OSN axons in providing low-resistance pathways for CSF flow.

claim: Increased resistance to CSF outflow could trigger a downregulation in CSF production and turnover.
source: Thus, damage to or decreases in the numbers of the OSN axons could increase the resistance to CSF outflow, triggering a downregulation in CSF production and turnover.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on logical inference from the known homeostatic regulation of CSF production in response to outflow changes.

claim: The anatomy of the cribriform plate has been studied in humans and other large mammals.
source: While the anatomy of the CP has been studied in humans (Kalmey et al., 1998) and other large mammals, both extinct and extant (Pihlström et al., 2005; Bhatnagar and Kallen, 1974; Bird et al., 2014; Bird et al., 2018), the structure of the mouse CP has not been as well characterized.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kalmey et al., 1998; Pihlström et al., 2005; Bhatnagar and Kallen, 1974; Bird et al., 2014; Bird et al., 2018, which provide external evidence for prior CP anatomical studies.

claim: The structure of the mouse cribriform plate has not been as well characterized as in humans and other large mammals.
source: While the anatomy of the CP has been studied in humans (Kalmey et al., 1998) and other large mammals, both extinct and extant (Pihlström et al., 2005; Bhatnagar and Kallen, 1974; Bird et al., 2014; Bird et al., 2018), the structure of the mouse CP has not been as well characterized.
evidence: The claim is based on a comparison of the existing literature, which shows more extensive studies in humans and large mammals than in mice.

claim: The side of the cribriform plate adjacent to the olfactory bulb is convex to accommodate the rounded shape of the anterior ventral face of the olfactory bulbs.
source: The side of the plate adjacent to the olfactory bulb was not planar, but rather convex to accommodate the rounded shape of the anterior ventral face of the olfactory bulbs (Figure 1E); consequently, thin sections (like those obtained using traditional histology) will only contain a fraction of the structure.
evidence: The claim is supported by direct observation from micro-CT imaging shown in Figure 1E, which provides visual evidence of the convex structure.

claim: A calcified ridge (crista galli) is observed along the midline of the cribriform plate.
source: We observed a calcified ridge along the midline of the CP (crista galli) with an irregular perforation pattern, with many small (<200 µm diameter) foramina (holes).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct observation from micro-CT imaging of mouse skulls.

claim: The cribriform plate has many small foramina less than 200 µm in diameter.
source: We observed a calcified ridge along the midline of the CP (crista galli) with an irregular perforation pattern, with many small (<200 µm diameter) foramina (holes).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct observation and measurement from micro-CT imaging of mouse skulls.

claim: There are four major foramina appearing in the same locations in all mice imaged.
source: While the positioning, number, and size of the smaller foramina were variable across mice, there were four major foramen appearing in the same locations in all mice imaged.
evidence: The claim is supported by direct observation from micro-CT imaging across multiple mice (n=6).

claim: Bilateral foramina are located on the anterior aspect of the cribriform plate, lateral to the crista galli.
source: Bilateral foramina were located on the anterior aspect of the plate, lateral to the crista galli, and midway along the dorsal ventral axis of the CP on each side (Figure 1C,D,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct observation from micro-CT imaging and photographs shown in Figures 1C, D, and F.

claim: The location and structure of the major foramina were consistent across all animals examined with micro-CT.
source: Their location and structure were consistent across all animals examined with micro-CT.
evidence: The claim is supported by direct observation from micro-CT imaging across multiple mice (n=6).

claim: The total area of the foramina in the mouse cribriform plate is 1.88 ± 0.29 mm².
source: We found the total area of the foramina was 1.88 ± 0.29 mm2 (mean ± std, n = 6, pooling both C57BL/6J and Swiss Webster mice) and the total area of the plate was 9.76 ± 1.12 mm2 (mean ± std, n = 6, pooling both C57BL/6J and Swiss Webster mice), similar to previous reports (Bird et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from micro-CT imaging of 6 mice, with statistical analysis (mean ± std).

claim: The total area of the cribriform plate in mice is 9.76 ± 1.12 mm².
source: We found the total area of the foramina was 1.88 ± 0.29 mm2 (mean ± std, n = 6, pooling both C57BL/6J and Swiss Webster mice) and the total area of the plate was 9.76 ± 1.12 mm2 (mean ± std, n = 6, pooling both C57BL/6J and Swiss Webster mice), similar to previous reports (Bird et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from micro-CT imaging of 6 mice, with statistical analysis (mean ± std), and is consistent with previous reports (Bird et al., 2018).

claim: CT images of C57BL/6J and Swiss Webster mice showed similar cribriform plate morphology.
source: CT images with C57BL/6J and Swiss Webster mice showed similar CP morphology (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D), suggesting that for these two strains, there are minimal strain differences.
evidence: The claim is supported by direct comparison of micro-CT images from both strains shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: A significant difference in total plate area was observed between C57BL/6J and Swiss Webster mice.
source: While a significant difference in total plate area (Figure 1G) was observed between C57BL/6J (10.693 ± 0.374 mm2) and Swiss Webster mice (8.821 ± 0.607 mm2), no significant difference was observed for total foramina area (Figure 1G) or in the ratio of foramina area to plate area (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements and statistical analysis (t(4) = 4.55, p=0.021, n = 3 for each group) shown in Figure 1G.

claim: No significant difference in total foramina area was observed between C57BL/6J and Swiss Webster mice.
source: While a significant difference in total plate area (Figure 1G) was observed between C57BL/6J (10.693 ± 0.374 mm2) and Swiss Webster mice (8.821 ± 0.607 mm2), no significant difference was observed for total foramina area (Figure 1G) or in the ratio of foramina area to plate area (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements and statistical analysis (t(4) = 1.32, p=0.256, n = 3 for each group) shown in Figure 1G.

claim: No significant difference in the ratio of foramina area to plate area was observed between C57BL/6J and Swiss Webster mice.
source: While a significant difference in total plate area (Figure 1G) was observed between C57BL/6J (10.693 ± 0.374 mm2) and Swiss Webster mice (8.821 ± 0.607 mm2), no significant difference was observed for total foramina area (Figure 1G) or in the ratio of foramina area to plate area (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements and statistical analysis (t(4) = 0.3891, p=0.7170, n = 3 for each group) shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The bone of the cribriform plate is impermeable to fluid movement.
source: Because the bone is impermeable to fluid movement, these holes will be the only outlet for CSF flow through the CP, and the nature of the soft tissue filling them (olfactory nerves, blood vessels, or lymphatic vessels) will play an important role in directing the flow of CSF.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the impermeability of bone tissue to fluid.

claim: The foramina in the cribriform plate are the only outlet for CSF flow through the plate.
source: Because the bone is impermeable to fluid movement, these holes will be the only outlet for CSF flow through the CP, and the nature of the soft tissue filling them (olfactory nerves, blood vessels, or lymphatic vessels) will play an important role in directing the flow of CSF.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the impermeability of bone and the presence of foramina.

claim: OMP-expressing OSN axon bundles traverse the cribriform plate and synapse onto the olfactory bulb.
source: OMP-expressing OSN axon bundles were observed traversing the CP and synapsing onto the olfactory bulb (Figure 1L,M), with two major axon bundles (yellow arrows) on the left and right sides (Figure 1L).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical staining with OMP antibody shown in Figures 1L and M.

claim: There are two major OSN axon bundles on the left and right sides of the cribriform plate.
source: OMP-expressing OSN axon bundles were observed traversing the CP and synapsing onto the olfactory bulb (Figure 1L,M), with two major axon bundles (yellow arrows) on the left and right sides (Figure 1L).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical staining with OMP antibody shown in Figure 1L, with yellow arrows indicating the two major bundles.

claim: OSN axon bundles fill the four major foramina observed in the cribriform plate.
source: These OSN axon bundles filled the four major foramen observed in the CP (Figure 1C,D,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation of immunohistochemical staining with micro-CT imaging shown in Figures 1C, D, and F.

claim: Smaller OSN axon bundles traverse the cribriform plate through smaller foramina bordering the crista galli.
source: In the coronal plane, smaller axon bundles traversed the CP through the smaller foramina bordering the crista galli (Figure 1M).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 1M.

claim: There are two distinct types of foramina in the cribriform plate: major foramina through which larger OSN bundles pass, and smaller holes with variable positioning.
source: These results show that there are two distinct types of foramen in the CP: the major foramen, through which the larger OSN bundles pass through, and a multitude of smaller holes whose position varied across animals and some of which carried smaller OSN bundles.
evidence: The claim is supported by direct observations from micro-CT imaging and immunohistochemistry across multiple mice.

claim: Extracellular fluid flow preferentially moves parallel to axon tracts.
source: Because extracellular fluid flow preferentially moves parallel to axon tracts (Syková and Nicholson, 2008), these nerves can provide directed conduits for CSF to move from the cranial cavity into the nasal cavity.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Syková and Nicholson, 2008, which provides external evidence for directional fluid flow along axon tracts.

claim: OSN axons can provide directed conduits for CSF to move from the cranial cavity into the nasal cavity.
source: Because extracellular fluid flow preferentially moves parallel to axon tracts (Syková and Nicholson, 2008), these nerves can provide directed conduits for CSF to move from the cranial cavity into the nasal cavity.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the known properties of fluid flow along axon tracts and the anatomical positioning of OSN axons.

claim: Blood vessels were found to run parallel to OSNs traversing the cribriform plate.
source: FITC-albumin filled vessels were found to run parallel to the OSNs traversing the CP (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by FITC-albumin vascular labeling shown in Figures 2D and E.

claim: Blood vessels labeled by DiI were visible in the smaller foramina of the cribriform plate.
source: Blood vessels, labeled by DiI, were also clearly visible in the smaller foramina (Figure 2M–O).
evidence: The claim is supported by DiI vascular labeling shown in Figures 2M-O.

claim: Both olfactory nerve bundles and blood vessels are present in foramina of the cribriform plate.
source: Both olfactory nerve bundles and blood vessels were present in other foramina (Figure 2M).
evidence: The claim is supported by combined immunohistochemical and vascular labeling shown in Figure 2M.

claim: Blood vessels traverse the cribriform plate in rodents.
source: These results are consistent with previous work showing blood vessels traverse the CP in the rodent (Lochhead and Thorne, 2012), much like the ethmoidal arteries and veins observed in humans (Lochhead and Thorne, 2012; Knudsen et al., 1989; Yang et al., 2009; Souza et al., 2009; Tsutsumi et al., 2016; Tsutsumi et al., 2019), linking the vascular territories of the nasal epithelia and brain.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lochhead and Thorne, 2012 and other studies, which provide external evidence for blood vessels traversing the CP.

claim: Ethmoidal arteries and veins traverse the cribriform plate in humans.
source: These results are consistent with previous work showing blood vessels traverse the CP in the rodent (Lochhead and Thorne, 2012), much like the ethmoidal arteries and veins observed in humans (Lochhead and Thorne, 2012; Knudsen et al., 1989; Yang et al., 2009; Souza et al., 2009; Tsutsumi et al., 2016; Tsutsumi et al., 2019), linking the vascular territories of the nasal epithelia and brain.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lochhead and Thorne, 2012; Knudsen et al., 1989; Yang et al., 2009; Souza et al., 2009; Tsutsumi et al., 2016; Tsutsumi et al., 2019, which provide external evidence for ethmoidal vessels in humans.

claim: Aquaporins greatly enhance the permeability of cells to water.
source: Aquaporins (AQP) greatly enhance the permeability of cells to water (Takata et al., 2004), and their presence would help facilitate the movement of fluid down the pressure gradient.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Takata et al., 2004, which provides external evidence for the water permeability function of aquaporins.

claim: The presence of aquaporins would help facilitate the movement of fluid down the pressure gradient.
source: Aquaporins (AQP) greatly enhance the permeability of cells to water (Takata et al., 2004), and their presence would help facilitate the movement of fluid down the pressure gradient.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the known function of aquaporins in enhancing water permeability.

claim: Different aquaporin protein subtypes have similar structure but differ in their localization throughout the body.
source: The different aquaporin protein subtypes have similar structure, but differ in their localization throughout the body (Takata et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Takata et al., 2004, which provides external evidence for aquaporin structure and localization patterns.

claim: Expression of AQP1 in the CNS begins early in development.
source: We first looked at the expression of aquaporin-1 (AQP1), as it has been shown that expression of AQP1 in the CNS begins early (Johansson et al., 2005; Weller et al., 2018), and is required in adulthood to maintain CSF production by the choroid plexus (Oshio et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Johansson et al., 2005; Weller et al., 2018, which provide external evidence for early AQP1 expression in the CNS.

claim: AQP1 is required in adulthood to maintain CSF production by the choroid plexus.
source: We first looked at the expression of aquaporin-1 (AQP1), as it has been shown that expression of AQP1 in the CNS begins early (Johansson et al., 2005; Weller et al., 2018), and is required in adulthood to maintain CSF production by the choroid plexus (Oshio et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Oshio et al., 2005, which provides external evidence for the role of AQP1 in CSF production.

claim: AQP1 is expressed along the periphery of the olfactory bulb in neonatal mice.
source: Interestingly, previous work has also shown that AQP1 is expressed along the periphery of the olfactory bulb in neonatal mice (Shields et al., 2010), and there are high levels of expression of AQP1, 3, and 5, within the nasal cavity (Ablimit et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shields et al., 2010, which provides external evidence for AQP1 expression in neonatal olfactory bulbs.

claim: There are high levels of expression of AQP1, 3, and 5 within the nasal cavity.
source: Interestingly, previous work has also shown that AQP1 is expressed along the periphery of the olfactory bulb in neonatal mice (Shields et al., 2010), and there are high levels of expression of AQP1, 3, and 5, within the nasal cavity (Ablimit et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ablimit et al., 2006, which provides external evidence for aquaporin expression in the nasal cavity.

claim: High levels of AQP1 expression were observed on the olfactory nerve layer down to the glomeruli.
source: We observed high levels of AQP1 expression on the olfactory nerve layer down to the glomeruli, as observed previously (Shields et al., 2010), and in the lamina propria of the neuroepithelium at both the medial (Figure 2F–G) and dorsal (Figure 2H–K) junctions of the olfactory bulb and nerve.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical staining shown in Figures 2F-K and is consistent with previous observations (Shields et al., 2010).

claim: AQP1 was observed in the lamina propria of the neuroepithelium at the medial and dorsal junctions of the olfactory bulb and nerve.
source: We observed high levels of AQP1 expression on the olfactory nerve layer down to the glomeruli, as observed previously (Shields et al., 2010), and in the lamina propria of the neuroepithelium at both the medial (Figure 2F–G) and dorsal (Figure 2H–K) junctions of the olfactory bulb and nerve.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical staining shown in Figures 2F-K.

claim: AQP1 was observed lining the foramina of the cribriform plate along the crista galli.
source: AQP1 was also observed lining the foramina of the CP along the crista galli (Figure 2L,N–O) but did not co-label with Vimentin-positive fibroblasts (Figure 2 – figure supplement J-K).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical staining shown in Figures 2L and 2N-O.

claim: AQP1 did not co-label with Vimentin-positive fibroblasts in the cribriform plate foramina.
source: AQP1 was also observed lining the foramina of the CP along the crista galli (Figure 2L,N–O) but did not co-label with Vimentin-positive fibroblasts (Figure 2 – figure supplement J-K).
evidence: The claim is supported by double immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1J-K.

claim: AQP1-expressing cells at the olfactory nerve-bulb junction might be olfactory ensheathing cells.
source: Based on previous reports (Au et al., 2002; Kumar et al., 2018) and our own results, we hypothesize that these AQP1-expressing cells might be olfactory ensheathing cells (OECs).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on inference from previous reports (Au et al., 2002; Kumar et al., 2018) and the authors' own immunohistochemical data.

claim: High levels of AQP1 expression were not seen in any other brain area except the choroid plexus.
source: High levels of AQP1 expression were not seen in any other brain area, with the exception of the choroid plexus (Johansson et al., 2005) strongly suggesting the interface between the olfactory nerve and bulb is a brain region with a high fluid flux flowing through it.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' immunohistochemical observations across brain regions and is consistent with previous reports (Johansson et al., 2005).

claim: The interface between the olfactory nerve and bulb is a brain region with high fluid flux.
source: High levels of AQP1 expression were not seen in any other brain area, with the exception of the choroid plexus (Johansson et al., 2005) strongly suggesting the interface between the olfactory nerve and bulb is a brain region with a high fluid flux flowing through it.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the localized high expression of AQP1, which is known to facilitate water movement.

claim: AQP4 is enriched around astrocyte endfeet in the cortex.
source: We then examined the expression of AQP4, which is enriched around astrocyte endfeet in the cortex (Nielsen et al., 1997) and is hypothesized to play a role in transport of fluid through the glymphatic system (Iliff et al., 2012) (though this is controversial [Smith et al., 2017]).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nielsen et al., 1997, which provides external evidence for AQP4 localization in astrocyte endfeet.

claim: AQP4 is hypothesized to play a role in transport of fluid through the glymphatic system.
source: We then examined the expression of AQP4, which is enriched around astrocyte endfeet in the cortex (Nielsen et al., 1997) and is hypothesized to play a role in transport of fluid through the glymphatic system (Iliff et al., 2012) (though this is controversial [Smith et al., 2017]).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Iliff et al., 2012, which provides external evidence for the hypothesized role of AQP4 in the glymphatic system, though the authors note this is controversial (Smith et al., 2017).

claim: The role of AQP4 in glymphatic fluid transport is controversial.
source: We then examined the expression of AQP4, which is enriched around astrocyte endfeet in the cortex (Nielsen et al., 1997) and is hypothesized to play a role in transport of fluid through the glymphatic system (Iliff et al., 2012) (though this is controversial [Smith et al., 2017]).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2017, which provides external evidence for controversy regarding AQP4's role in glymphatic transport.

claim: AQP4 expression was observed in GFAP-positive astrocytes in the cortex.
source: We observed expression of AQP4 in GFAP-positive astrocytes in the cortex (Figure 2 – figure supplement L-M) and within the olfactory nerve and neuroepithelium (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by double immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1L-M.

claim: AQP4 expression was observed within the olfactory nerve and neuroepithelium.
source: We observed expression of AQP4 in GFAP-positive astrocytes in the cortex (Figure 2 – figure supplement L-M) and within the olfactory nerve and neuroepithelium (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-G.

claim: Expression of AQP2, AQP3, and AQP5 was limited to the neuroepithelium and cribriform plate.
source: The localization of other aquaporins, AQP2, AQP3, and AQP5, were also examined at the olfactory bulb and nerve junction, but their expression was limited to the neuroepithelium and CP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–E,H–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-E and H-I.

claim: The highly enriched expression of aquaporins at the olfactory nerve-bulb junction could provide a low-resistance pathway for fluid to pass from the olfactory bulb to the olfactory nerves.
source: The highly enriched expression of aquaporins observed in the tissues at the junctional area of the olfactory nerve and bulb could provide a low-resistance pathway for fluid to pass from the olfactory bulb to the olfactory nerves, out of the cranium, and ultimately into the nasal cavity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed aquaporin expression patterns and the known function of aquaporins in facilitating water movement.

claim: Lymphatic vessels play a role in moving fluid throughout the body.
source: Lymphatic vessels play a role in moving fluid throughout the body and are found in the meninges (Aspelund et al., 2015; Louveau et al., 2015) and nasal epithelium (Johnston et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about lymphatic vessel function, supported by citations.

claim: Lymphatic vessels are found in the meninges.
source: Lymphatic vessels play a role in moving fluid throughout the body and are found in the meninges (Aspelund et al., 2015; Louveau et al., 2015) and nasal epithelium (Johnston et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aspelund et al., 2015; Louveau et al., 2015, which provide external evidence for meningeal lymphatic vessels.

claim: Lymphatic vessels are found in the nasal epithelium.
source: Lymphatic vessels play a role in moving fluid throughout the body and are found in the meninges (Aspelund et al., 2015; Louveau et al., 2015) and nasal epithelium (Johnston et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Johnston et al., 2004, which provides external evidence for lymphatic vessels in the nasal epithelium.

claim: Lymphatic vessels crossing the cribriform plate could play a role in transporting fluid from the cranial cavity to the nasal cavity.
source: Lymphatic vessels crossing the CP could play a role in transporting fluid from the cranial cavity to the nasal cavity.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on logical inference from the known function of lymphatic vessels and their potential anatomical positioning.

claim: Blood vessel endothelial cells expressing LYVE1 were observed throughout the brain.
source: Surprisingly, we observed blood vessel (identified by FITC-albumin fills) endothelial cells that expressed LYVE1 throughout the brain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by double labeling with FITC-albumin and LYVE1 shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-G.

claim: Non-lymphatic cells of unknown type expressing LYVE1 were observed in the frontal cortex.
source: We also observed non-lymphatic cells of an unknown type in the frontal cortex expressing LYVE1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) that were GFAP, NeuN, Oligo1, and CD164 negative (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–E,H–M).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical characterization shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: LYVE1-positive vessels were found adjacent to OSNs in the nasal cavity.
source: Interestingly, we found a few LYVE1+ vessels (both DiI and FITC-albumin negative) adjacent to OSNs in the nasal cavity (Figure 3D–G), lining holes in the lamina propria of the neuroepithelium, and traversing the CP (Figure 3H–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by LYVE1 labeling shown in Figures 3D-G.

claim: LYVE1-positive vessels were found lining holes in the lamina propria of the neuroepithelium.
source: Interestingly, we found a few LYVE1+ vessels (both DiI and FITC-albumin negative) adjacent to OSNs in the nasal cavity (Figure 3D–G), lining holes in the lamina propria of the neuroepithelium, and traversing the CP (Figure 3H–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by LYVE1 labeling shown in Figures 3H-K.

claim: LYVE1-positive vessels were found traversing the cribriform plate.
source: Interestingly, we found a few LYVE1+ vessels (both DiI and FITC-albumin negative) adjacent to OSNs in the nasal cavity (Figure 3D–G), lining holes in the lamina propria of the neuroepithelium, and traversing the CP (Figure 3H–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by LYVE1 labeling shown in Figures 3H-K.

claim: LYVE1-positive lymphatic vessels traverse the cribriform plate and could facilitate the movement of fluid from the brain compartment to the nasal compartment.
source: Although LYVE1 is not expressed exclusively in lymphatic vessels, these results demonstrate that LYVE1+ lymphatic vessels traverse the CP and could facilitate the movement of fluid from the brain compartment to the nasal compartment.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed LYVE1+ vessels that do not co-label with blood vessel markers, combined with the known function of lymphatic vessels.

claim: Intranasal treatment of ZnSO4 causes rapid death of OSNs that persists for months.
source: Previous work has shown that intranasal treatment of ZnSO4 causes the rapid death of OSNs, and persists for months (Burd, 1993; McBride et al., 2003; Stewart et al., 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Burd, 1993; McBride et al., 2003; Stewart et al., 1983, which provide external evidence for the effects of ZnSO4 on OSNs.

claim: A loss of the olfactory nerve layer and overall reduction in the size of the olfactory bulb indicates successful ablation of OSNs by ZnSO4.
source: Because a loss of the olfactory nerve layer and overall reduction in the size of the olfactory bulb indicates successful ablation of OSNs by ZnSO4 (Burd, 1993), we measured the size of the olfactory bulb 2, 10, and 30 days after zinc treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Burd, 1993, which provides external evidence for indicators of successful OSN ablation.

claim: A significant decrease in olfactory bulb area was observed 10 days after ZnSO4 treatment compared to vehicle controls.
source: A significant decrease in olfactory bulb area was observed compared to vehicle controls 10 days (t(12) = 6.46, p≤0.001, n = 14 (7 each group), ttest2) and 30 days (t(12) = 6.712, p≤0.001, n = 7 for each group, ttest2) after treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements and statistical analysis (t(12) = 6.46, p≤0.001) shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A significant decrease in olfactory bulb area was observed 30 days after ZnSO4 treatment compared to vehicle controls.
source: A significant decrease in olfactory bulb area was observed compared to vehicle controls 10 days (t(12) = 6.46, p≤0.001, n = 14 (7 each group), ttest2) and 30 days (t(12) = 6.712, p≤0.001, n = 7 for each group, ttest2) after treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements and statistical analysis (t(12) = 6.712, p≤0.001) shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mice treated with ZnSO4 exhibited weight loss initially after treatment.
source: Mice treated with ZnSO4 exhibited weight loss initially after treatment, but then began gaining weight at a normal rate starting one week later (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by weight measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Mice treated with ZnSO4 began gaining weight at a normal rate starting one week after treatment.
source: Mice treated with ZnSO4 exhibited weight loss initially after treatment, but then began gaining weight at a normal rate starting one week later (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by weight measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ZnSO4 treatment had minimal effects on running behavior compared to vehicle controls.
source: Running wheels (Med Associates Inc, Fairfax, VT) were placed in the cages of individually-housed mice (Figure 6B) to quantify activity levels before and after treatment. ZnSO4 treatment had minimal effects on running behavior (Figure 6C–D), compared to vehicle controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by running wheel activity measurements shown in Figures 6C-D.

claim: Chemical ablation of OSNs with ZnSO4 had minimal effects on the overall health and behavior of mice.
source: These results show that chemical ablation of OSNs with ZnSO4 had minimal effects on the overall health and behavior of the mice.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the weight and activity data showing recovery and normal behavior patterns.

claim: Two days after ZnSO4 treatment, the beginnings of degeneration of olfactory nerves were observed.
source: Two days after ZnSO4 treatment (Figure 6G), we observed the beginnings of degeneration of the olfactory nerves.
evidence: The claim is supported by OMP immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Ten days after ZnSO4 treatment, a profound loss of OSN axons was observed.
source: Ten days after ZnSO4 treatment (Figure 6H), we observed a profound loss of OSN axons, and 30 days after treatment, a complete loss of OSNs traversing the CP from the nasal epithelium was observed (Figure 6I).
evidence: The claim is supported by OMP immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Thirty days after ZnSO4 treatment, a complete loss of OSNs traversing the cribriform plate from the nasal epithelium was observed.
source: Ten days after ZnSO4 treatment (Figure 6H), we observed a profound loss of OSN axons, and 30 days after treatment, a complete loss of OSNs traversing the CP from the nasal epithelium was observed (Figure 6I).
evidence: The claim is supported by OMP immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 6I.

claim: A significant decrease in OMP signal was observed in ZnSO4-treated animals compared to vehicle controls.
source: A significant decrease in OMP signal was observed in the treated animals compared to the vehicle controls (F(3, 32)=259.5, p≤0.001, n = 14 for vehicle, n = 5 for 2 day, n = 8 for 10 day, and n = 9 for 30 day, one-way ANOVA).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence measurements and statistical analysis (F(3, 32)=259.5, p≤0.001) shown in Figure 6N.

claim: OSNs have largely degenerated 10 days after ZnSO4 treatment.
source: These results show that OSNs have largely degenerated 10 days after treatment and are absent a month after intranasal ZnSO4 treatment.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the OMP immunohistochemical and quantitative fluorescence data.

claim: OSNs are absent a month after intranasal ZnSO4 treatment.
source: These results show that OSNs have largely degenerated 10 days after treatment and are absent a month after intranasal ZnSO4 treatment.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the OMP immunohistochemical and quantitative fluorescence data.

claim: No appreciable changes in mRNA levels of AQP1, Klotho, NF-κβ, or RelA were found 2 days after ZnSO4 treatment.
source: However, we found no appreciable changes in mRNA levels or GFAP expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) 2 or 10 days after ZnSO4 treatment, indicating there is no inflammatory response in the cranial cavity following treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: No appreciable changes in GFAP expression were found 2 or 10 days after ZnSO4 treatment.
source: However, we found no appreciable changes in mRNA levels or GFAP expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) 2 or 10 days after ZnSO4 treatment, indicating there is no inflammatory response in the cranial cavity following treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C and F.

claim: There is no inflammatory response in the cranial cavity following ZnSO4 treatment.
source: However, we found no appreciable changes in mRNA levels or GFAP expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) 2 or 10 days after ZnSO4 treatment, indicating there is no inflammatory response in the cranial cavity following treatment.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the lack of changes in inflammatory markers (mRNA levels and GFAP expression).

claim: No significant change in LYVE1 expression or localization was found 2 days after ZnSO4 treatment.
source: We found no significant change in LYVE1 expression or localization 2 days after ZnSO4 treatment in LYVE1-GFP mice (Figure 5K), however, a change in localization at 10 and 30 days after treatment was observed (Figure 5L–M).
evidence: The claim is supported by LYVE1 imaging shown in Figure 6K (labeled as Figure 5K in the text).

claim: A change in LYVE1 localization was observed 10 and 30 days after ZnSO4 treatment.
source: We found no significant change in LYVE1 expression or localization 2 days after ZnSO4 treatment in LYVE1-GFP mice (Figure 5K), however, a change in localization at 10 and 30 days after treatment was observed (Figure 5L–M).
evidence: The claim is supported by LYVE1 imaging shown in Figures 6L-M (labeled as Figures 5L-M in the text).

claim: ZnSO4 treatment ablates OSNs while not affecting neighboring lymphatic vessel density in the cribriform plate area.
source: These results show that ZnSO4 treatment ablates OSNs while not affecting neighboring lymphatic vessel density in the CP area.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined observations of OSN loss and maintained LYVE1+ vessel presence.

claim: Evans blue injected into the cisterna magna was not observed within the sagittal sinus or the parenchyma.
source: EB was not observed within the sagittal sinus or the parenchyma, consistent with EB not crossing the glia limitans.
evidence: The claim is supported by direct observation from Evans blue injection experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Evans blue injected into the cisterna magna was restricted to the subarachnoid space around the brain and spinal column.
source: Dye was restricted to the subarachnoid space around the brain and spinal column (Figure 4B–C) and was also clearly visible in the nasal epithelium and the deep cervical lymph nodes (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct observation from Evans blue injection experiments shown in Figures 4B-C.

claim: Evans blue injected into the cisterna magna was clearly visible in the nasal epithelium and deep cervical lymph nodes.
source: Dye was restricted to the subarachnoid space around the brain and spinal column (Figure 4B–C) and was also clearly visible in the nasal epithelium and the deep cervical lymph nodes (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct observation from Evans blue injection experiments shown in Figures 4D-E.

claim: Cardiac perfusion had no qualitative effect on Evans blue movement.
source: Cardiac perfusion had no qualitative effect on EB movement, as EB was present in the nasal epithelia even without perfusion.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of Evans blue distribution with and without perfusion.

claim: The observed pathways of CSF flow and drainage through the cribriform plate are consistent with previous work using radiolabeled tracers, latex fills, and other tracers.
source: The observed pathways of CSF (EB dye) flow and drainage through the CP, into the deep cervical lymph nodes, and along the spinal column, are consistent with previous work using radiolabeled tracers, latex fills, and other tracers (Bradbury et al., 1981; Johnston et al., 2004; Cserr et al., 1992b; Pizzo et al., 2018; Hubbs et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of the authors' Evans blue data with previous studies cited (Bradbury et al., 1981; Johnston et al., 2004; Cserr et al., 1992b; Pizzo et al., 2018; Hubbs et al., 2012).

claim: 3kDa-FITCDextran injected into the cisterna magna was observed draining into the nasal cavity along the olfactory nerve.
source: 3kDa-FITCDextran was observed draining into the nasal cavity along the olfactory nerve (Figure 5D–F), and co-localizing with LYVE1+ vessels along the olfactory nerve (Figure 5G–I), although the dye did not appear to be concentrated in the LYVE1+ vessels.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence imaging shown in Figures 5D-F.

claim: 3kDa-FITCDextran injected into the cisterna magna co-localized with LYVE1-positive vessels along the olfactory nerve.
source: 3kDa-FITCDextran was observed draining into the nasal cavity along the olfactory nerve (Figure 5D–F), and co-localizing with LYVE1+ vessels along the olfactory nerve (Figure 5G–I), although the dye did not appear to be concentrated in the LYVE1+ vessels.
evidence: The claim is supported by double fluorescence imaging shown in Figures 5G-I.

claim: CSF exits the cranial cavity through the cribriform plate and is absorbed by nasal LYVE1-positive vessels.
source: These results show that CSF exits the cranial cavity through the CP and is absorbed by nasal LYVE1+ (putatively lymphatic) vessels.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the tracer injection experiments showing dye movement through the CP and into LYVE1+ vessels.

claim: Ablation of OSNs blocks CSF outflow through the cribriform plate.
source: Thus, ablating OSNs blocks CSF outflow through the CP, and this blockage persists for a least a month.
evidence: The claim is supported by tracer injection experiments comparing vehicle and ZnSO4-treated mice shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The blockage of CSF outflow through the cribriform plate after OSN ablation persists for at least a month.
source: Thus, ablating OSNs blocks CSF outflow through the CP, and this blockage persists for a least a month.
evidence: The claim is supported by tracer injection experiments at 30 days post-treatment shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Ten days after ZnSO4 treatment, the peak location and center of mass of the Evans blue dye curve was shifted caudally relative to vehicle controls.
source: We found that 10 and 30 days after treatment, the peak location and center of mass of the dye curve was shifted caudally in ZnSO4-treated mice, relative to vehicle controls, indicating that CSF outflow through the CP was decreased by OSN ablation.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of Evans blue distribution shown in Figures 7H-J with statistical analysis.

claim: Thirty days after ZnSO4 treatment, the peak location and center of mass of the Evans blue dye curve was shifted caudally relative to vehicle controls.
source: We found that 10 and 30 days after treatment, the peak location and center of mass of the dye curve was shifted caudally in ZnSO4-treated mice, relative to vehicle controls, indicating that CSF outflow through the CP was decreased by OSN ablation.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of Evans blue distribution shown in Figures 7H-J with statistical analysis.

claim: CSF outflow through the cribriform plate was decreased by OSN ablation.
source: We found that 10 and 30 days after treatment, the peak location and center of mass of the dye curve was shifted caudally in ZnSO4-treated mice, relative to vehicle controls, indicating that CSF outflow through the CP was decreased by OSN ablation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the caudal shift in dye distribution, which indicates reduced forward movement of CSF through the CP.

claim: Significant interactions between the effects of time after treatment and treatment type on the center of mass location were observed for the side ipsilateral to treatment.
source: For the side ipsilateral to treatment, we saw significant interactions between the effects of time after treatment and the treatment type (ZnSO4 or vehicle) on the center of mass location (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Table 1 (F=5.45, d.o.f.=2, P=0.0086).

claim: Significant effects on the center of mass were observed by both the duration of treatment and the type of treatment.
source: We also saw significant effects on the center of mass and the anterior-posterior peak location by both the duration of treatment and the type of treatment (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Significant effects on the anterior-posterior peak location were observed by both the duration of treatment and the type of treatment.
source: We also saw significant effects on the center of mass and the anterior-posterior peak location by both the duration of treatment and the type of treatment (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by two-way ANOVA statistical analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: No difference in Evans blue collected in the deep cervical lymph nodes was observed between vehicle- and zinc-treated mice 30 days after treatment.
source: No difference in EB collected in the deep cervical lymph nodes was observed between vehicle- (Figure 8B) and zinc-treated (Figure 8C) mice 30 days after treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by visual comparison of Evans blue in lymph nodes shown in Figures 8B-C.

claim: The decrease in CSF outflow through the cribriform plate in zinc-treated mice was still observed 30 days after treatment despite increases in infusion volume and duration.
source: Interestingly, the decrease in CSF outflow through the CP in zinc-treated mice, compared to vehicle mice, was still observed 30 days after treatment (Figure 8D–E), despite the increases in infusion volume and duration.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of Evans blue distribution shown in Figures 8D-G.

claim: A significant decrease in outflow of 3kDa-FITCDextran into the nasal cavity in ZnSO4-treated mice relative to vehicle controls was observed.
source: A significant decrease in outflow of 3kDa-FITCDextran into the nasal cavity in ZnSO4-treated mice, relative to vehicle controls, was also observed (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of 3kDa-FITCDextran distribution shown in Figure 9F-G with statistical analysis.

claim: An increase in outflow resistance will drive a rise in ICP unless there is a compensatory reduction of CSF production or changes in the resistance of other outflow pathways.
source: The production and outflow of CSF is dynamically balanced (Marmarou et al., 1975) in such a way that an increase in outflow resistance will drive a rise in ICP (Kosteljanetz, 1987; Jones, 1985), unless there is a compensatory reduction of CSF production or changes in the resistance of other outflow pathways.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Marmarou et al., 1975; Kosteljanetz, 1987; Jones, 1985, which provide external evidence for CSF dynamics and ICP regulation.

claim: Kaolin injections into the cisterna magna produce elevations in ICP.
source: Injections of kaolin into the cisterna magna are known to produce elevations in ICP, and are used to generate an animal model of hydrocephalus (Bloch et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bloch et al., 2006, which provides external evidence for kaolin-induced ICP elevation.

claim: ICP significantly increased during locomotion 2 days after kaolin injections into the cisterna magna compared to aCSF controls.
source: We found that 2 days after kaolin injections into the cisterna magna ICP significantly increased during locomotion (Table 2) compared to aCSF controls (Figure 10B–C), but not during rest.
evidence: The claim is supported by ICP measurements and statistical analysis (t(4) = 5.88, p=0.0042) shown in Figure 10C and Table 2.

claim: No statistically significant difference in ICP was observed in ZnSO4-treated mice at rest or during locomotion compared to vehicle controls.
source: No statistically significant difference was observed in ZnSO4-treated mice at rest or during locomotion as compared to the vehicle controls (Figure 10B–C) measured 10, 30, and 60 days after treatment (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ICP measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 10B-C and Table 2.

claim: Despite the blockage of the nasal CSF outflow pathway, ICP did not increase after OSN ablation.
source: Despite the blockage of the nasal CSF outflow pathway, ICP did not increase.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the ICP measurements showing no significant difference between ZnSO4-treated and vehicle control mice.

claim: The lack of ICP rise when the nasal outflow pathway is blocked suggests that an alternate outflow route is taken and/or CSF production is decreased.
source: This suggests that an alternate outflow route is taken and/or CSF production is decreased.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on logical inference from the observation that ICP did not rise despite blocked outflow.

claim: A significant decrease in the distance Evans blue traveled along the spinal column was observed 10 days after ZnSO4 treatment.
source: While no significant difference between the vehicle and ZnSO4 treatment groups in the distance of dye traveled 2 days after treatment was observed, a significant decrease in the distance traveled was observed for both 10 and 30 days after treatment (Figure 10H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of dye travel distance and statistical analysis (t(12) = 5.069, p=0.00028) shown in Figure 10H.

claim: A significant decrease in the distance Evans blue traveled along the spinal column was observed 30 days after ZnSO4 treatment.
source: While no significant difference between the vehicle and ZnSO4 treatment groups in the distance of dye traveled 2 days after treatment was observed, a significant decrease in the distance traveled was observed for both 10 and 30 days after treatment (Figure 10H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of dye travel distance and statistical analysis (t(9) = 4.571, p=0.00134) shown in Figure 10H.

claim: In response to the disruption of the nasal outflow pathway, there was a decrease in CSF flow down the spinal cord.
source: Our results show that in response to the disruption of the nasal outflow pathway there was a decrease in CSF flow down the spinal cord.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the decreased distance of Evans blue travel along the spinal column after ZnSO4 treatment.

claim: The foramina permit the flow of fluid out of the brain through the intercellular space between OSN axons, blood vessels, and LYVE1-positive vessels traversing through them.
source: The foramina will permit the flow of fluid out of the brain through the intercellular space between OSN axons, blood vessels, and LYVE1+ vessels traversing through them.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the anatomical observations of structures within the foramina and the known properties of fluid flow.

claim: A highly stereotyped pattern in the positioning of the major foramina was observed across mice.
source: We observed a highly stereotyped pattern in the positioning of the major foramina across mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by micro-CT imaging observations across multiple mice (n=6).

claim: The routes of OSNs may be predisposed to go through either the dorsal or ventral foramina depending on their receptor group and target glomeruli.
source: It is tempting to speculate that the routes of the OSNs are predisposed to go through either the dorsal or ventral foramina depending on their receptor group and target glomeruli (Buck and Axel, 1991; Feinstein and Mombaerts, 2004; Rodriguez-Gil et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observed stereotyped pattern and previous knowledge about OSN organization (Buck and Axel, 1991; Feinstein and Mombaerts, 2004; Rodriguez-Gil et al., 2010).

claim: AQP1 was localized to the olfactory bulb and nerve junction and lining the foramina of the cribriform plate, instead of AQP4.
source: We found that aquaporin-1 (AQP1) was localized to the olfactory bulb and nerve junction and lining the foramina of the CP, instead of aquaporin-4 (AQP4), which is the dominant water channel in the CNS (Nagelhus and Ottersen, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical observations shown in Figure 2 and comparison with AQP4 distribution.

claim: AQP4 is the dominant water channel in the CNS.
source: We found that aquaporin-1 (AQP1) was localized to the olfactory bulb and nerve junction and lining the foramina of the CP, instead of aquaporin-4 (AQP4), which is the dominant water channel in the CNS (Nagelhus and Ottersen, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nagelhus and Ottersen, 2013, which provides external evidence for AQP4 as the dominant CNS water channel.

claim: Instead of a rise in ICP as expected due to blockage of CSF drainage into the nasal cavity, no change in ICP was observed after OSN ablation.
source: Interestingly, instead of a rise in ICP as would be expected due to a blockage of CSF drainage into the nasal cavity, we observed no change in ICP.
evidence: The claim is supported by ICP measurements comparing ZnSO4-treated and vehicle control mice shown in Figure 10.

claim: The lack of ICP rise could not be explained by an increase in drainage of CSF down the spinal cord pathway.
source: This could not be explained by an increase in drainage of CSF down the spinal cord pathway, as we observed a similar reduction in CSF flow down this pathway following ZnSO4 treatment.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation of decreased CSF flow down the spinal cord after ZnSO4 treatment.

claim: Other drainage pathways might become engaged and/or reduce their outflow resistance to compensate for the blockage of the cribriform plate outflow.
source: The first is that other drainage pathways become engaged and/or reduce their outflow resistance to compensate for the blockage of the cribriform plate outflow.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis proposed to explain the lack of ICP rise despite blocked nasal outflow.

claim: A re-routing of CSF flow in a more rostral direction would account for the decreased flow down the spinal cord.
source: A re-routing of CSF flow in a more rostral direction would account for the decreased flow down the spinal cord.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on logical inference to explain the observed decrease in spinal CSF flow.

claim: Some outflow pathways have thresholds for opening.
source: Some outflow pathways have thresholds for opening (Welch and Friedman, 1960), and these might become engaged following ZnSO4 treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Welch and Friedman, 1960, which provides external evidence for threshold-dependent outflow pathways.

claim: CSF production is not a passive process but rather one under active neural control.
source: CSF production is not a passive process, but rather one under active neural control (Lindvall et al., 1978; Edvinsson and Lindvall, 1978; Tuor et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lindvall et al., 1978; Edvinsson and Lindvall, 1978; Tuor et al., 1990, which provide external evidence for neural control of CSF production.

claim: There are likely homeostatic processes that sense ICP and cause compensatory increases or decreases in CSF production.
source: As ICP needs to be maintained within a healthy range, there are likely homeostatic processes that sense ICP, and cause compensatory increases or decreases in CSF production, similar to other mechanosensory processes in other organs of the body (Umans and Liberles, 2018; Guild et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on inference from the need for ICP homeostasis and comparison with other mechanosensory systems (Umans and Liberles, 2018; Guild et al., 2018).

claim: ASIC3 channels are expressed in the ventricles and are sensitive to changes in pressure that are physiologically relevant to ICP regulation.
source: A potential mechanism mediating this feedback is mechanically sensitive ASIC3 channels, which are expressed in the ventricles (Jalalvand et al., 2018), and are sensitive to changes in pressure that are physiologically relevant to ICP regulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jalalvand et al., 2018, which provides external evidence for ASIC3 channel expression and pressure sensitivity.

claim: Pathological elevations of ICP due to trauma produce a rise in systemic blood pressure and a decrease in heart rate, known as the Cushing response.
source: Pathological elevations of ICP due to trauma produce a rise in systemic blood pressure and a decrease in heart rate, known as the Cushing response (Hoff and Reis, 1970; Doba and Reis, 1972), showing the brain has a way of sensing ICP (Hoff and Reis, 1970), and pressure-sensitive brain regions mediating these responses have been identified (Hoff and Reis, 1970; Doba and Reis, 1972).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hoff and Reis, 1970; Doba and Reis, 1972, which provide external evidence for the Cushing response.

claim: The brain has a way of sensing ICP.
source: Pathological elevations of ICP due to trauma produce a rise in systemic blood pressure and a decrease in heart rate, known as the Cushing response (Hoff and Reis, 1970; Doba and Reis, 1972), showing the brain has a way of sensing ICP (Hoff and Reis, 1970), and pressure-sensitive brain regions mediating these responses have been identified (Hoff and Reis, 1970; Doba and Reis, 1972).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the existence of the Cushing response, supported by citations to Hoff and Reis, 1970; Doba and Reis, 1972.

claim: A similar response to the Cushing response may be occurring in the choroid plexus to compensate for decreased CSF drainage after ZnSO4 treatment.
source: A similar response may be occurring in the choroid plexus to compensate for the decreased CSF drainage we observe after ZnSO4 treatment, thus, avoiding the rise in ICP that is normally associated with a decrease in CSF drainage (Lindvall et al., 1978; Edvinsson and Lindvall, 1978).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on inference from the observed lack of ICP rise and comparison with known ICP sensing mechanisms.

claim: The CSF drainage observed in dye injection experiments may differ in the awake animal compared to anesthetized animals.
source: Our dye injections were done under anesthesia and the CSF drainage observed may differ in the awake animal.
evidence: The claim is an acknowledgment of a potential limitation based on known effects of anesthesia on physiological processes.

claim: A significant decrease in CSF drainage due to OSN ablation was observed despite the limitation of anesthesia during dye injections.
source: Although these limitations should be considered, since we observed a difference in drainage between the ZnSO4- and vehicle-treated mice, this should still be considered a significant decrease in CSF drainage due to OSN ablation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the consistent differences observed between treatment groups despite potential anesthesia effects.

claim: The LYVE1 mouse model exhibited some non-lymphatic specific LYVE1 expression in vascular endothelial cells in the brain.
source: Although our lymphatic mouse model (Lyve1.Cre.GFP mice crossed with Ai6 or Ai14 reporter lines) exhibited some non-lymphatic specific LYVE1 expression in vascular endothelial cells in the brain, there were also LYVE1+ vessels along the olfactory nerve that did not co-label with vascular perfusion markers (FITC-albumin fills or DiI staining) and that absorbed dye injected into the cisterna magna.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations from double labeling experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: LYVE1-positive vessels along the olfactory nerve that did not co-label with vascular perfusion markers are putatively lymphatic vessels that transport CSF out of the cranial cavity.
source: These vessels are putatively lymphatic vessels that transport CSF out of the cranial cavity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the lack of co-labeling with blood vessel markers and the absorption of CSF tracers.

claim: Previous work has shown transport of fluid across the cribriform plate.
source: Previous work has shown that there is transport of fluid across the CP (Bradbury et al., 1981) and acute blockage of the plate (by sealing it with cyanoacrylate glue) blocks transport of radiolabeled albumin (Bradbury and Westrop, 1983) establishing the CP as a route of CSF drainage, which then drains into the nasal lymphatics (Erlich et al., 1986; Weller et al., 1992; Koh et al., 2006; Nagra et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2017; Kida et al., 1993; Walter et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2019; Ethell, 2014; Pizzo et al., 2018; Cserr and Patlak, 1992c; Papaiconomou et al., 2002; Johnston et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bradbury et al., 1981 and other studies, which provide external evidence for fluid transport across the CP.

claim: Acute blockage of the cribriform plate by sealing it with cyanoacrylate glue blocks transport of radiolabeled albumin.
source: Previous work has shown that there is transport of fluid across the CP (Bradbury et al., 1981) and acute blockage of the plate (by sealing it with cyanoacrylate glue) blocks transport of radiolabeled albumin (Bradbury and Westrop, 1983) establishing the CP as a route of CSF drainage, which then drains into the nasal lymphatics (Erlich et al., 1986; Weller et al., 1992; Koh et al., 2006; Nagra et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2017; Kida et al., 1993; Walter et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2019; Ethell, 2014; Pizzo et al., 2018; Cserr and Patlak, 1992c; Papaiconomou et al., 2002; Johnston et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bradbury and Westrop, 1983, which provides external evidence for blockage of albumin transport.

claim: CSF drains through the cribriform plate into the nasal lymphatics.
source: Previous work has shown that there is transport of fluid across the CP (Bradbury et al., 1981) and acute blockage of the plate (by sealing it with cyanoacrylate glue) blocks transport of radiolabeled albumin (Bradbury and Westrop, 1983) establishing the CP as a route of CSF drainage, which then drains into the nasal lymphatics (Erlich et al., 1986; Weller et al., 1992; Koh et al., 2006; Nagra et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2017; Kida et al., 1993; Walter et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2019; Ethell, 2014; Pizzo et al., 2018; Cserr and Patlak, 1992c; Papaiconomou et al., 2002; Johnston et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Erlich et al., 1986; Weller et al., 1992; Koh et al., 2006; Nagra et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2017; Kida et al., 1993; Walter et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2019; Ethell, 2014; Pizzo et al., 2018; Cserr and Patlak, 1992c; Papaiconomou et al., 2002; Johnston et al., 2005) that provide external evidence for CSF drainage into nasal lymphatics.

claim: This work elucidates the anatomical basis of CSF transport through the cribriform plate and its role in CSF turnover.
source: Our work elucidates the anatomical basis of CSF transport through the CP and its role in CSF turnover, and demonstrates that damage to the olfactory sensory nerves can impair this pathway.
evidence: The claim is based on the comprehensive anatomical and functional data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Damage to olfactory sensory nerves can impair the CSF transport pathway through the cribriform plate.
source: Our work elucidates the anatomical basis of CSF transport through the CP and its role in CSF turnover, and demonstrates that damage to the olfactory sensory nerves can impair this pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by the ZnSO4 ablation experiments showing decreased CSF outflow after OSN damage.

claim: This work provides a possible mechanism for the observed correlations between neurodegeneration, anosmia, and environmental toxins like air pollution.
source: This work provides a possible mechanism for the observed correlations between neurodegeneration, anosmia, and environmental toxins like air pollution.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the demonstrated role of OSNs in CSF drainage and the known exposure of OSNs to environmental toxins.

claim: Olfactory impairment occurs during normal aging.
source: Although olfactory impairment, or anosmia, occurs during normal aging (Doty and Kamath, 2014; Murphy et al., 2002), anosmia frequently precedes many neurological disorders (Talamo et al., 1989; Talamo et al., 1991; Kovács, 2004; Roberts et al., 2016; Zou et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Doty and Kamath, 2014; Murphy et al., 2002, which provide external evidence for age-related olfactory impairment.

claim: Anosmia frequently precedes many neurological disorders.
source: Although olfactory impairment, or anosmia, occurs during normal aging (Doty and Kamath, 2014; Murphy et al., 2002), anosmia frequently precedes many neurological disorders (Talamo et al., 1989; Talamo et al., 1991; Kovács, 2004; Roberts et al., 2016; Zou et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Talamo et al., 1989; Talamo et al., 1991; Kovács, 2004; Roberts et al., 2016; Zou et al., 2016, which provide external evidence for anosmia as a precursor to neurological disorders.

claim: Studies have shown correlations between levels of air pollution and olfactory impairment.
source: Furthermore, studies have shown correlations with the levels of air pollution with olfactory impairment (Ajmani et al., 2016; Doty and Hastings, 2001; Adams et al., 2016; Imamura and Hasegawa-Ishii, 2016; Cheng et al., 2016) and neurodegenerative disease pathology, such as Alzheimer's disease (Calderón-Garcidueñas et al., 2004; Calderón-Garcidueñas et al., 2012; Calderón-Garcidueñas et al., 2016a; Calderón-Garcidueñas et al., 2016b; Chen et al., 2017a; Chen et al., 2017b), although the mechanism behind these correlations is unclear.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ajmani et al., 2016; Doty and Hastings, 2001; Adams et al., 2016; Imamura and Hasegawa-Ishii, 2016; Cheng et al., 2016, which provide external evidence for correlations between air pollution and olfactory impairment.
